title: Invisible academics and the challenges of being an independent scholar
summary:
Why is academic research still tied so closely to universities? Discover the challenges facing independent scholars

The post Invisible academics and the challenges of being an independent scholar appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Charlotte Fawcett, former HEPI Policy Intern.

For many academics, their institution may feel like a source of frustration: conflicting and unclear working policies; mandated annual training; and requirements for how much time to spend in the office. However, as researchers unaffiliated with an academic institution have found, it is much easier to publish research attached to a university than to be without one.

What is an academic? The Oxford English Dictionary includes the following definition of an academic:

A member of a university or college, now spec. a senior member, a member of a university or college’s teaching or research staff. Also in a weakened sense: a person interested in or excelling at pursuits involving reading, thinking, and study.

This demonstrates the importance given to an institutional affiliation when defining academics, thus excluding those who are independent scholars.

An independent scholar is defined as someone who conducts scholarly research outside universities and traditional academia. Being an independent scholar can result in a multitude of issues, from a lack of access to academic resources to problems accessing research funding. The former can include an inability to access physical spaces, such as laboratories, as well as digital spaces, with online research articles behind paywalls. All of this impacts the independent scholar’s ability to conduct research. Ironically, to access the Oxford English Dictionary definition above, an institutional login was required.

Additionally, independent scholars who are interested in conducting surveys or other research with human participants may face limitations in receiving ethics approval, something which can restrict where findings may be published in academic literature. Independent scholars may also struggle without the added benefit of institutional credibility.

The term independent scholars can cover a broad range of individuals conducting research, including museum and gallery curators; archaeologists working in the field; professional services staff; and even members of the public. Some of these individuals may have access to institutional services through collaborations or partnerships, whilst others do not. There is therefore a wide range of differing experiences under the umbrella of independent scholars.

The question then is, why has academic research been restricted to universities? One reason is logistical – having physical research spaces such as libraries and laboratories together in proximity allows researchers to streamline the academic process. However, there are also considerations of accountability – academics may be funded by public money and are therefore required to produce output demonstrating the use of such money. The Research Excellence Framework (REF), which assesses research excellence, can also be used as an accountability measure, demonstrating the quality and impact of institutional research and its value for money.

If an institution or organisation was created to allow independent scholars access to some of the benefits of universities but also ensured accountability, would this give independent scholars an equal standing to those who are institutionally affiliated?

Similar programmes have existed before in other sectors – the Lonely Goat running club was launched to bring together solo runners into a shared community. The set-up of this group also gives them dedicated spaces at the London Marathon, allowing the group to take part on equal standing with other running clubs. Since 2016, the Olympics have also had the Refugee Olympic Team, allowing displaced individuals to compete in the Olympics. This gives them the ability to continue to compete in sporting events to the highest level, despite not being affiliated with a specific country.

The Lonely Goat running club emerged organically through a grassroots, community-led effort, whereas the Refugee Olympic Team was established through a top-down initiative led by Olympic President Thomas Bach. These examples demonstrate that successful independent communities can be created through either approach.

Although this principle has previously been applied to sporting events, it could be used in other contexts, including academia, by establishing a body that independent scholars can become affiliated with, giving them equal rights and responsibilities to those working at academic institutions.

Establishing a home for independent scholars and ensuring that they are considered on equal footing encourages more inclusivity in research, allowing a more diverse group of individuals to be recognised for their contributions to research, including community participants.

Universities have historically been the primary home of academic research because they provide shared infrastructure, resources, and accountability mechanisms tied to public funding. But can independent scholars achieve equal standing through alternative models that offer similar support and oversight outside traditional institutions? Although questions remain about how this could be established, sporting models demonstrate how collective structures can legitimise and enable participation for unaffiliated individuals and point toward new possibilities for recognising and supporting independent scholars.

title: Calls grow ‘to flunk’ Portugal’s education minister amid exam marking fiasco
summary:
Fernando Alexandre’s push to digitise marking process deemed a failure with some students and parents contemplating legal action

Pressure is growing on Portugal’s education minister to resign amid student and teacher protests over his handling of this year’s national school exams.

Fernando Alexandre is accused of failing to take responsibility for what critics say is an unprecedented and chaotic school exam season affecting children aged 14 to 18, prompting student protesters to call for him “to be flunked”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Pressure is growing on Portugal’s education minister to resign amid student and teacher protests over his handling of this year’s national school exams.

Fernando Alexandre is accused of failing to take responsibility for what critics say is an unprecedented and chaotic school exam season affecting children aged 14 to 18, prompting student protesters to call for him “to be flunked”.

At the centre of the controversy, which has plunged the Portuguese education sector into its worst crisis in decades, is Alexandre’s push to fully digitise the process for marking exams.

The centre-right government said the shift was necessary to modernise Portugal’s public administration and make school evaluations “more rigorous and objective” for the more than 260,000 students taking exams in primary and secondary schools.

But many parents, teachers and students have graded the change a failure and some people are contemplating pursuing legal action against the state. About 19,000 people have signed a petition calling for the annulment of all of this year’s results.

The principal of one of the largest school groups in Portugal, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said: “I struggle to trust in the process after everything that happened.”

In the weekly newspaper Expresso, the journalist and political commenter Daniel Oliveira decried the “inexplicable chaos” of the process, attacked Alexandre’s “unspeakable display of incompetence”, and said the credibility of the entire examination system had been “mortally wounded”.

It didn’t take long for the cracks to show in the new system, in which digitised, anonymous questions were distributed randomly to teachers and the grading professors’ remit was changed.

From the start of the exam season in mid-June, schools reported errors in the allocation of papers, with retired teachers and at least one dead teacher being called to mark them. Some educators were told to mark subjects out of their areas of expertise.

While grading the exams, several teachers reported difficulty accessing the marking platform, missing continuation pages, incomplete student answers, illegible scanned images and students’ answers disappearing from the online system.

André Azinheira, 32, a secondary school maths teacher, said he had received clear instructions to grade answers despite uncertainty over whether he was assessing a student’s full submission or whether pages were missing.

He said: “I knew someone could be wrong, but I had no way of knowing if pages were indeed missing, so I had to do my part. I may have hurt students or not, I have no idea. But I predicted there would be several errors in the grades.”

The Guardian heard of other cases in which teachers expressed similar dilemmas.

Reacting to growing unease from schools and students, Alexandre blamed staff for failing to “remove staples from the tests”, supposedly complicating the digitisation process. He dismissed teachers’ complaints about errors in the digital marking platform as insignificant or “false”.

After the results were released, three days late in mid-July, thousands of students complained about extreme discrepancies between their predicted grades and the posted exam grades, with some realising their grades were still missing.

Upon requesting access to a copy of the exam, several students reported finding missing pages, unknown handwriting and answers due to switched tests, and, in some cases, lost exams. Some students with special educational needs have complained that during the digitisation of the tests, the tags identifying those additional needs were left out, potentially affecting the grading.

An education watchdog later said that 26,000 exams had been affected by software or “parameterisation” errors, and that more than 18,000 grades were being changed.

Requests for re-evaluation of national high school exams have already exceeded 20,000, three times more than last year, according to data revealed by the minister of education this week. Every re-evaluation process has a cost of €25 (£21) a test, and the payment has to be made by the student.

After witnessing his friends and colleagues’ stress over switched and missing papers and exam grades, Raul Noetzold, 18, created a students’ movement called Chumbado.pt to call for Alexandre’s resignation. Last Friday, hundreds of students, parents, teachers and members of several opposition parties protested outside the education ministry.

Luciana Almeida, 18, would have attended the protest but she lives and studies in Penafiel, a three-and-a-half-hour drive from Lisbon. Almeida said she had not received a grade for the Portuguese exam she took in June. After her classmates received theirs, she discovered her paper had got lost in a pile of undigitised exams and she had been forced to repeat the test.

“I worked hard and I feel cheated because they lost my test,” said Almeida. “I feel at a disadvantage compared with others. And it will be hard for me to trust the new results … These college applications won’t be fair. It’s our future that’s at stake and the ministry of education is ruining it.”

Last week, an embattled Alexandre announced that students affected by software errors would not be awarded less than the minimum pass mark. But some teachers are not happy about that decision, saying in some cases it will unfairly affect students’ college applications.

And many parents remain furious. Rita Reino, 53, president of the parents’ association of Camões high school in Lisbon, said: “At this stage there is no fair solution. The state has violated the principles of equality and fairness. We want to hold the state accountable; we want to sue the state.”

The fiasco is proving politically damaging for the government, although the prime minister, Luís Montenegro, has so far resisted calls to fire Alexandre. A recent survey found that seven out of 10 Portuguese are deeply unhappy with the government and cite the exam debacle as one of the leading causes of dissatisfaction.

In a statement, the education ministry acknowledged that the “disruptions in implementation” had caused “instability in the education system and anxiety among students and families”, which it said it regretted.

It added: “Despite the constraints of the first phase, the process is now proceeding in the second phase without significant problems, and on the third day of grading more than 65% of the tests had already been graded.”

Asked about the calls for Alexandre to resign, the ministry said: “Calls for resignation are part of the public, political and democratic debate. However, given the situation, the priority of the ministry of education was to identify the problems, correct them quickly, and ensure that no student is harmed in their school career or access to higher education.”

title: GOP Rift Over Education Department’s Future
summary:
GOP Rift Over Education Department’s Future
jessica.blake@… Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

In a 13-to-9 vote Thursday, two Republicans sided with the Democrats to protect four key education offices.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
In a rebuke of President Trump’s efforts to shutter the Education Department, a Senate committee voted Thursday to block the White House from outsourcing the responsibilities of four key ED offices to other federal agencies.

The bill, which advanced to the Senate floor following the 13-to-9 vote, specifically protects programs within the offices of special education, elementary and secondary education, postsecondary education, and Indian education.

Those are fewer than half of the education offices affected by the 14 interagency agreements signed so far, and many education advocates hope to see them all blocked. But Sen. Tim Kaine, the Virginia Democrat who sponsored the bill, said that while he would love to reach a bipartisan consensus on the other offices, this is a strong step forward for now.

Kaine’s willingness to block some but not all of the interagency agreements was key to securing support from Republican co-sponsors Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, from Maine and Alaska, respectively, who crossed party lines to help the minority advance the bill.

“We ended up working with each other over the course of the last month and reached an accord,” Kaine said. “We quickly find areas of agreement, and when we’re not on the same page on things, we set those aside. But I think this particular bill would maintain core components within [the Education Department].”

Other offices not addressed in Thursday’s bill include the Office for Civil Rights, which transferred to the Department of Justice, and the Office of Career and Technical Education, which transferred to the Department of Labor. Sen. Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat, attempted to block all agreements and the OCR one specifically—but neither of those amendments passed. (The one Murray amendment that did pass with nearly unanimous support would require the Education Department to provide quarterly reports on the cost of each agreement compared to the previous cost of executing the same functions within ED.)

So while the legislation is unlikely to advance any more—as House Republicans and many in the Senate continue to back Trump’s plan—the committee vote demonstrates a growing rift among the congressional GOP over the president’s interagency agreements and the future of the federal government’s role in higher ed.

Trump loyalists like Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama argued that the Department of Education is failing to properly serve students and that moving offices to other agencies would change that.

“The definition of losing is doing the same thing over and over … and we’re losing—we’re losing badly,” he said. “So why are we defending this? I don’t understand it.”

Other Republicans filed amendments seeking to abolish the department, but those plans didn’t receive a vote Thursday. Similarly, Republicans in the House advanced legislation this month that would make the transfer of ED’s responsibilities permanent.

But Collins and Murkowski, both of whom have challenged the White House at times during Trump’s second term, argue that Congress placed these offices and grant programs under the Education Department for a reason and that moving them puts students at risk.

“This bill is straightforward. It keeps the administration of important, landmark education programs at the Department of Education, where Congress specifically put them and where they belong,” Collins said.

Murkowski added, “We cannot lose sight of the fact that at the end of the day we’re talking about children.”

The committee chair, Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, didn’t vote in favor of the bill, saying he’s “not in favor of stripping the administration’s authority to streamline efforts … carte blanche.” But he did voice support for a provision that would block the interagency agreement sending special education services to the Department of Health and Human Services.

“Moving [special education] to HHS would be a mistake. It shifts special education from an educational and civil rights model to a medical model, treating students with disabilities as patients to diagnose rather than learners to educate,” said Cassidy who worked as a doctor for decades before entering politics. “I’m a conservative. I think smaller government is better government, but I worry that many states are still struggling with [special education] requirements and need federal technical assistance, coordination and oversight.”

Cassidy introduced his own separate bill that would only block the special ed agreement but decided not to bring it to a vote because it would be “subsumed” by Kaine’s bill.

“I’ve not been able to use the word ‘subsumed’ during my entire chairmanship, so thank you for giving me the opportunity,” he said to Kaine as the room laughed.

​​​Emmanual Guillory, senior director of government relations at the American Council on Education, noted that as chairman, Cassidy could have blocked Kaine’s bill from even reaching a vote, especially since knew that it was likely to pass with support from Collins and Murkowski. Yet he let it happen—a move Guillory described as one of “integrity and character.”

“It’s him realizing that he is a part of the greater whole and wanting to have a democratic process in the fairest way possible,” Guillory said.

The Trump administration continued to defend the agreements after the committee meeting. In a letter sent to Congress, Education Secretary Linda McMahon stressed that the Trump administration has no plan of backing off in its attempt to “wind down” the Education Department. Rather, she’s asked lawmakers for “continued support.”

“Since these agreements were signed … they have demonstrated measurable results by driving stronger grant competitions, streamlining government operations, and producing better outcomes for Americans,” McMahon wrote. “The evidence is clear: these agreements are not expanding bureaucracy; they are correcting failures that too often put process ahead of performance, and ultimately, the American people.”

title: A Green Mountain College Resurrection?
summary:
A Green Mountain College Resurrection?
Josh Moody Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

An evangelist wants to reopen a closed campus in rural Vermont. But the finances and strategy are unclear, and his prior attempt at running a college raises questions.

Byline(s)
Josh Moody
full_text:
Tommie Zito wants a revival for Green Mountain College.

And for America.

The self-described “itinerant evangelist” is in talks to purchase the Green Mountain campus in rural Vermont, which closed in 2019 and was later purchased by whiskey distiller Raj Bhakta, who said he wanted to hand the campus over to someone with a vision for “the revival of the United States and Western Civilization.” Zito fit the bill: He aims to open Z University on the site, the first of a proposed international network of campuses with an emphasis on biblical education and evangelism.

In a Thursday morning livestream, Zito described the planned opening of the Vermont campus as the launch of a major undertaking, promising that “schools will open up all over the globe” in the coming years.

“It’s going to happen fast,” Zito said. “But it had to be in America first.”

Zito, who did not respond to interview requests from Inside Higher Ed, is hoping to succeed where Bhakta failed; his revitalization effort, which envisioned a campus hotel and distillery, never got off the ground. Bhakta announced in February that he planned to give the campus away. But after issuing a request for proposals, he changed course and now plans to sell the Green Mountain campus to Zito instead.

(The deal has not yet closed but is reportedly expected to be finalized by Oct. 1.)

Zito has not specified a purchase price but has told other media outlets that he’s getting the campus at a fair price. But even if Bhakta gives Zito a plum deal on the property, questions abound about how the new institution will be funded. And Zito’s past—he founded and led a Bible college in Florida that operated only briefly—shows a history of grand promises that failed to materialize and outsize claims that cannot be independently verified.

While Zito’s higher ed journey is unique, his push to take over a defunct campus illuminates the challenges such properties pose for local communities, which must weigh the promise of revitalization against the risk of further deterioration.

Before Z University

Zito’s first attempt at launching a college dates back 15 years.

Zito, who says he began his ministry in 1996, first posted on his website in 2011 that he planned to open a Bible college that August. But those plans—and associated promises—changed over time.

Public records in Florida, where Zito lives, show he registered the name Freedom College in early 2012. Archived versions of his website show that Zito eventually settled on the name Zoe Bible College, which he announced in 2013 would open in January 2014 and offer degrees in areas such as audio and video production, sound design, cinematography, and film production. Zito noted in the post that Zoe would partner with Patten University, a private Christian institution located in California, on that effort.

(The president of Patten at that time did not respond to a request for comment from Inside Higher Ed sent via LinkedIn. Patten closed in 2020, though an unaffiliated university formerly known as American Graduate University rebranded with the same name in 2022.)

Zito finally opened Zoe Bible College in August 2015 with a narrower academic portfolio than envisioned. Instead of media production classes, Zoe was centered around more traditional topics for a Bible school. An archived list of course offerings shows the curriculum appeared to draw heavily from the free plug-and-play curriculum developed by Harvestime International Network, which provides resources to Bible schools. Numerous course titles match Harvestime’s catalog, including Spiritual Warfare and Strategies for Spiritual Harvest.

It is unclear when Zoe Bible College, which advertised a two-year program as of its 2015 start date, ultimately shut down. But a Facebook post notes that the institution produced three graduates in 2017.

In response to questions Inside Higher Ed asked during Thursday’s livestream, Zito said he had to “push pause on the college” because ultimately he “wasn’t satisfied with the product.” He noted “physical brick-and-mortar challenges,” which prompted the college to move locations several times.

Both the college and Zito’s website repeated false claims that the school was “fully accredited.” However, Zito conceded that was untrue during the livestream.

“It was never fully accredited,” Zito said. “Maybe there’s a misinterpretation of that.”

For the new Z University slated to open in fall 2027, Zito has said that he plans to pursue accreditation from the New England Commission of Higher Education. But NECHE President Larry Schall told Inside Higher Ed by email he has heard “absolutely nothing” from Zito.

“It takes years and there’s no guarantee a new institution would meet our standards,” he wrote.

Big Plans, Limited Resources

Though the purchase price remains unknown, Zito told The New York Post that he had received a $1 million donation to use as a down payment. (Bhakta bought the campus for $4.5 million.)

In Bhakta’s request for proposals issued earlier this year, he noted that the new owner would need to budget “$1.5 million per year to maintain existing infrastructure and to … catch up on deferred maintenance.” That estimate does not include labor and other costs of running a college.

But publicly available financial documents for Zito’s ministry, registered as American Awakening Inc., show a modest operation lacking the sort of capital to launch and sustain a university. In fiscal year 2021, the latest year available, the nonprofit organization had $98,028 in revenue, expenses of $94,706 and net income of $3,322. American Awakening’s highest year for net income on record was fiscal 2017, when it made $33,341.

Another nonprofit registered as Tommie Zito Ministries was dissolved in 2011. Court records show that before the organization shut down it declared Chapter 7 bankruptcy in 2010 and owed creditors nearly $1 million, including more than $225,000 to the Internal Revenue Service.

Zito’s past also reveals a propensity for making grandiose promises and unverified claims.

His ministry’s claims have grown more exaggerated over the years. His website indicates that American Awakening has orchestrated more than 14,000 services and led four million souls to Christ “over the past two decades.” By the numbers, that adds up to at least 700 services a year, with 200,000 souls won annually—or approximately two or more services and 548 conversions every day.

In 2014, American Awakening announced that Zito would star in a reality show dubbed The Evangelistz, which would follow him, his wife and their children around “in their quest for souls.” Though the announcement said several major networks were interested, the project was never released.

In addition, an archived biography on Zito’s website in 2001 claimed he chose ministry over a career as a professional athlete, despite being “one of the best soccer players in the nation.” However, Zito is not listed on archived team rosters at West Virginia University, which he attended in the early 1990s before graduating from Rhema Bible Training Center in Oklahoma. Local media coverage of Zito’s purported athletic career is also lacking in the New Jersey region where he grew up and attended high school.

Challenges Ahead

Bhakta’s failed revamp of Green Mountain College has left some locals skeptical about prospects for the campus. One commenter on the livestream alleged that Bhakta made promises similar to Zito’s but “left us high and dry.” In response to a question about how he would gain the community’s trust, Zito said he would meet with locals to discuss their concerns.

Stephen Gavazzi, an Ohio State University professor and expert on town-gown relations, told Inside Higher Ed that building trust is just as challenging as addressing facilities and enrollment concerns. A key step, he said, is creating inroads with the community and communicating plans to local officials so they don’t hear about them via media reports.

“I think any founder who’s hoping to establish a new institution, especially in a small community that has already experienced the closure of a college, really has to demonstrate that they’re interested in becoming part of the local fabric rather than simply occupying the campus,” Gavazzi said.

Experts also noted that funding the college will be another major obstacle for Zito, who will need to navigate a turbulent and highly regulated industry.

“It doesn’t sound like this is a person who has knowledge of higher education processes,” Brian Weinblatt, founder of the advisory firm Higher Ed Consolidation Solutions, told Inside Higher Ed.

Weinblatt added that Zito would need to tap professionals with demonstrated expertise to help make his dream a reality. Even then, he questioned the wisdom of investing in a long-closed campus given the high costs of upkeep, deferred maintenance and recruiting challenges in the region.

But Zito’s pitch seems more centered on spiritual need than student demographics. In various videos posted to social media, Zito has emphasized the need for revival in the nation—especially in Vermont, which has one of the highest rates of nonbelievers among all 50 states.

He also referenced the spiritual needs of the region in his 2005 book, A Spiritual Awakening: How to Respond to the Emerging Hunger for God, showing it has long been a concern of his.

“If any part of America is indicative of what has happened to our church and our nation, it is by far New England,” Zito wrote about the region at the time. “This place where Puritans and Pilgrims once came to seek the Father earnestly, now has become the seat of liberalism. On grounds once set apart as Bible schools, perverted thinking and secular humanism abounds. The area overflows with witchcraft, homosexual lifestyles, and self-help groups.”

Zito intends to open the college in August and start his revival this fall.

title: Report: Struggling Florida High Schoolers Take CLT to Graduate
summary:
Report: Struggling Florida High Schoolers Take CLT to Graduate
Johanna Alonso Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
A USA Today report found that struggling high schoolers in Florida are taking the Classic Learning Test, a K–12 academic progress exam and alternative to the SAT and ACT that has been embraced by conservatives, to graduate. Students unable to pass the state’s algebra and English exams or score high enough on the SAT or ACT instead are opting to take the CLT.

Mathematics education experts who evaluated the test said the CLT’s math section had a higher concentration of middle school–level math than the SAT or the ACT. Officials in at least nine Florida school districts attributed the exam to increased graduation rates since the test was introduced in 2023. Leesa Crescenzi, the former head of the math department for the Hillsborough County School District in Tampa, told USA Today that students had discovered there were enough prealgebra questions on the test that they could pass simply by answering the easy questions and then selecting B for all the remaining questions.

In Hillsborough County, one school board member, Nadia Combs, argued that the test allows students who aren’t prepared for work or college to graduate high school.

“If they think they’re doing well and they’re passing,” she said, “but at the end of the day when they get a job or they go to college and they’re not able to do well on a typical test, that’s concerning.” Combs voted to offer the test to more graduating seniors.

Jeremy Tate, CEO of Classic Learning Initiatives, the company that administers the CLT, disputed the idea that the test is easier than the SAT and ACT. The state decides what a student must score on the test to graduate; for the CLT, they must score 11 out of a total of 40 points. State officials told USA Today that Classic Learning Initiatives recommended that number. Florida plans to raise that score slightly next year.

title: It’s Never Too Late to Go Back to College
summary:
It’s Never Too Late to Go Back to College
Joshua.Bay Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

In this week’s Voices of Student Success episode, ReUp CEO Terah Crews explores why students stop out and what colleges can do to help them return.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
For millions of Americans, leaving college isn’t the end of the story.

While many students stop out before earning a credential, they often plan to return. Yet re-enrolling can prove just as challenging as enrolling in the first place. As colleges look to re-enroll adults with some college but no credential, they are rethinking how to support students whose educational journeys aren’t linear.

Terah Crews, chief executive officer of ReUp Education, a national organization dedicated to helping adults navigate re-entry into higher education, joined Inside Higher Ed student success reporter Joshua Bay on Voices of Student Success to discuss why students stop out, what motivates them to return, the barriers colleges still place in their way and what it will take to build institutions that truly serve today’s adult learners.

Here are five takeaways for colleges working to better support adult learners returning to higher education.

Stopping out isn’t the end of a student’s college journey.

Crews said referring to students as “stop-outs” rather than “dropouts” better reflects the reality that, for most, leaving college is a pause, not a permanent decision to abandon higher education.

“Certainly there’s a subset of the population where that’s true, but the vast majority of learners stopped out because there was something going on in their life that kept them from continuing,” Crews said.

She noted that family responsibilities, health challenges, financial pressures and the general complexity of balancing college with life circumstances often interrupt students’ educational journeys.

“The most important thing to understand is most of these learners don’t quit thinking they’re never going to come back,” Crews said. “But once they’re out for about a semester, inertia takes over and it really gets challenging.”

Recognizing that is critical, she said; many institutions stop actively engaging students once they’ve been away for an extended period.

“This sort of nuance is really important because for the vast majority of institutions, they do nothing once learners have been out for more than a year,” Crews said.

Most stop-outs want to return, but colleges often make coming back harder than leaving.

Crews said students who stop out leave for a wide range of reasons, but institutions often overcomplicate the process of re-enrolling them by trying to solve every barrier before simply reconnecting with them.

“You don’t need to have a solution for every complexity in a person’s life on why they can’t come back, nor do you need to understand the unique situation that they’re in right now,” Crews said. “You simply need to start a conversation with them, and then you have to have the ability to actively serve them for, in some cases, a long period of time before they’re actually able to make that step back.”

She added that colleges also need to rethink how they view returning adult learners. Unlike many traditional-age students who are still weighing the value of higher education, most adults have already experienced firsthand what not having a credential can cost.

“We spend so much time talking about how younger generations aren’t valuing higher education the way that they used to, [but] adults are,” Crews said. “They are because they applied for that job and were told that they weren’t eligible because they didn’t have a bachelor’s degree or they didn’t have an associate degree or they didn’t have a credential.”

“This is a population where you don’t have to sell them on the value of higher education the way you would an 18-year-old,” she added. “They see it, they feel it, they know the barriers that are keeping them from economic security and opportunity in life.”

Adult learners need colleges designed around their lives.

Crews said many of the barriers institutions create for returning students stem from policies designed with the traditional 18-year-old college student in mind. Given that the average college student is now 31 years old, she argued that colleges should be designing systems around the realities of today’s learners.

“Maybe that hold on registration due to a parking ticket or a $200 fee makes sense for an 18-year-old because it’s the forcing mechanism to get somebody who’s still developing responsible behaviors to come in and pay their bill,” Crews said. “But for a 31-year-old, telling them you can’t come back because of a $200 bill that they forgot 10 years ago, it serves as a signal: ‘I don’t belong,’ or it serves as a signal of ‘You’re not interested, you’re not invested in me.’

“Moreover, it’s a bad financial decision for the institution,” she added. “Oftentimes when I’m talking to CFOs, they’re like, ‘Wait a minute, we have a policy that says if they owe $200, they can’t come back and pay us $4,000 in tuition. Who came up with that?’”

Crews said colleges can better support returning learners by removing unnecessary barriers, such as registration holds and application fees, streamlining admissions, and making it easier for students to understand how previously earned credits apply toward a degree.

“The easier you make it for them to take that first step, the more you will get back,” Crews said. “It’s really that simple.”

Flexible pathways are creating more ways back to college.

Crews said growing interest in short-term credentials, workforce pathways and prior learning assessment is creating more flexible entry points for adults returning to higher education. Rather than expect every student to re-enter through a traditional degree program, colleges are beginning to offer multiple pathways that better align with learners’ goals and circumstances.

“That’s really important because currently we’re not enrolling as many new stop-outs every year,” Crews said. “So if we want to really stem the tide and start shrinking that 40 million population, we’ve got to develop new solutions, new pathways for learners to get back in.”

She said short-term credentials, in particular, can help students improve their economic mobility while building toward a longer-term credential.

“If they can do that by pursuing some shorter-form credential that gets them a better job, more salary, more income while they’re pursuing a degree that’ll give them a pathway to a career, that’s an added benefit,” she said.

Returning is as much an emotional journey as an academic one.

Crews said re-enrollment is more than an administrative or financial decision. Many returning students also carry feelings of failure, shame or uncertainty that institutions often overlook.

Drawing on her own experience as both a high school and college stop-out, Crews said those emotions are common—and shouldn’t be mistaken for a lack of motivation.

“Many years ago, I was a high school stop-out, and then I was actually a college stop-out as well,” Crews said. “The more we realize it, the more we engage, the better we’re going to get at meeting people where they are and helping them realize that these fears, these anxieties, are OK. They’re normal, but they’re welcome.”

title: U.S. Universities Among 7 Approved to Set Up Greek Branch Campuses
summary:
U.S. Universities Among 7 Approved to Set Up Greek Branch Campuses
sara.custer@in… Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

Institutions from the U.S., U.K. and France have been given the go-ahead following a controversial change in the law governing private institutions.

Byline(s)
Seher Asaf for Times Higher Education
full_text:
Greece has granted licenses to seven universities from the U.S., U.K., France and Cyprus to set up international branch campuses in the country starting in the 2026–27 academic year.

The country’s Ministry of Education, Religious Affairs and Sports said in a press release that the permits were granted after “favourable opinions” from the National Authority for Higher Education and the National Organisation for the Certification of Qualifications and Vocational Guidance.

The newly approved universities are Georgetown University and Roger Williams University, which will operate as The American University of Greece; Iowa State University; and the European University Cyprus.

France’s Université Sorbonne Paris Nord and the U.K.’s University of Essex and University of Derby were “re-evaluated and cleared to continue,” the statement said.

Six of the seven will operate in Athens, while the Iowa State branch will be based in Thessaloniki.

The announcement comes more than two years after the Greek Parliament narrowly passed a bill allowing foreign universities to open branches in the country following weeks of student protests. Thousands of students and staff demonstrated outside the country’s Parliament, arguing that the changes would favor wealthy students while devaluing degrees from public universities.

Protesters feared that private institutions would offer higher salaries to staff and lower entry requirements for students, worsening public universities’ existing recruitment struggles.

Since the passing of the bill, the education ministry has granted permits to several foreign universities to establish branch campuses in the country. In August 2025, it announced that it was allowing the Open University, the University of York, the University of Keele and the University of Nicosia to open campuses in Athens and Thessaloniki.

“Last year we took the first step. This year we prove that this historic reform was not a single moment, but the compass for a new path in Greek Higher Education,” Minister of Education Sofia Zacharaki said in a press release.

“For us, the real issue has never been the confrontation between the public and non-public universities. On the contrary, we are simultaneously moving towards the greatest strengthening of the public university in recent decades.”

Greece’s deputy minister of education, Nikos Papaioannou, said the move would help address brain-drain issues.

“For decades, Greece remained one of the few countries in the world where the operation of non-state universities was not allowed, leading thousands of our young people abroad, weakening the international position of Greek higher education,” he said in the press release.

“Today, with one of the strictest institutional frameworks in Europe, the State ensures that non-state non-profit universities operate under strict academic supervision, with high quality standards.”

title: Personal Aphorisms
summary:
Personal Aphorisms
Sara Brady Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM

When in doubt …

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
A conversation with an old friend last week got me thinking about the phrases I fall back on when in doubt. We all have them, from sources high and low. I’ll share a few of my favorites, in hopes of inspiring my wise and worldly readers to chime in with some of theirs.

The Boy coined this one when he was about 12, having been benched for most of a Little League game that his team lost badly. It struck me as a fundamental truth. Think your college administration sucks? Step up and try it yourself. Think your political leaders suck? Run for something, or volunteer for a campaign. Think the larger discourse around higher ed sucks? Grab a keyboard or a microphone and jump in. You might or might not succeed, but honest failure doesn’t gnaw at the soul like riding the bench does.

Origin unknown, but again, it’s the truth. Often, in fact, the ones who think they might be wrong are the angriest of all when questioned or confronted precisely because they’re working so hard to hold the story together.

This is one of those truths that’s easy to say and tough to live, but it matters. One of the most emotionally satisfying moments of my career came years ago at a previous institution: A half dozen or so people were at a meeting that I was chairing. At one point, a senior member of the group declared that he was gravely offended by what a colleague had said, stood up and said he’d walk out. After a brief silence, I shrugged and resumed the discussion. A few seconds later, he sat down. Successfully calling a bluff is a great feeling.

Origin unknown. In the frantic whack-a-mole of solving a cascading series of problems, it’s sometimes more useful to stop, take a step back and look at the bigger picture. If people keep shortcutting a process, maybe the process itself is the problem. Leaders set a tone whether they mean to or not; if they’re frantic and nervous, that becomes the background noise of the culture. Sometimes the right play is to call a timeout.

Originally Immanuel Kant, though I came to it via Isaiah Berlin. It’s a helpful reminder.

Stephen Bronner, a former professor at Rutgers. I’d substitute another term for “proletariat,” but the point still stands. It’s why I’m glad that community colleges teach art and philosophy as well as more vocational subjects. Talent is much more evenly distributed than resources are; reserving the finer things only for those with resources is both unfair and a way of shortchanging the future. You never know where the next breakthrough will come from, so it’s best to cast the net wide.

Annie Dillard. I choose to read this as a useful admonition to get over oneself.

Ken Kesey, via Tom Wolfe. Sometimes you just need to commit one way or the other and live with what happens. Even the wrong decision can be less bad than indecision. As a mentor once told me, focus less on making the right decision and more on making the decision right.

title: Florida English Professor Fired for Teaching ‘Political’ Story Sues College
summary:
Florida English Professor Fired for Teaching ‘Political’ Story Sues College
Emma Whitford Fri, 07/31/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
English professor Vinita Prabhakar is suing South Florida State College after she was abruptly fired for teaching a story the college president deemed “political,” according to a complaint filed Wednesday in Florida district court.

Prabhakar assigned her freshman English students “Bettering Myself,” an award-winning story by Ottessa Moshfegh that centers on a Catholic school math teacher who drinks to excess and talks about sex with her students. One of her students told Prabhakar the story made them “a bit uncomfortable,” to which Prabhakar “acknowledged that the story could be difficult” and invited the student to talk more about it in class the next day, the complaint states.

At some point, the student who expressed discomfort spoke to another professor or administrator about the assignment, though “it is not known whether the student actually complained about the assignment or merely discussed the fact that the work had been assigned reading,” according to the complaint. An employee registered a complaint about the assignment, and Prabhakar learned from her department chair that the issue had “escalated.”

Following several days of back-and-forth with other administrators about the assignment, Prabhakar met with South Florida State President Fred Hawkins on Feb. 11. During the meeting, Hawkins said “he would not want his own college-aged daughter reading” the story, and that he didn’t “ever want to see this story again,” the complaint states. He also told Prabhakar he’d been in contact “with Tallahassee” and the Board of Trustees about the matter. Hawkins, who became president of the college in 2023, is a former Republican state legislator and an ally of Gov. Ron DeSantis.

A day later, college officials removed Prabhakar from the classroom and told her that her contract would not be renewed. When she asked why, a human resources director told Prabhakar it was because she taught a story that wasn’t in the textbook and that “the president has the final say.”

Prabhakar has taught “Bettering Myself” for a decade without incident, according to the complaint. She sued to “vindicate her constitutional and statutory rights” and seek reinstatement.

“For 20 years, I’ve taught students how to engage with stories that excite them, challenge them, and broaden their experience of what it means to be human,” Prabhakar said in a news release from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which is representing her. “I don’t plan on stopping now. If what happened to me becomes the norm, colleges across America will become less curious, less vibrant, and less free.”

Prabhakar joins a growing list of professors who have sued their institutions after being fired, alleging First Amendment violations.

Spokespeople for South Florida State did not return Inside Higher Ed’s request for comment.

title: The cliff is no longer coming. It is here, and international students are no longer a nice-to-have
summary:
Institutions that embed global recruitment at the heart of their planning will be best placed to weather the demographic downturn in the US, writes Paul Hofmann.

The post The cliff is no longer coming. It is here, and international students are no longer a nice-to-have appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
If you work in international education, you have probably spent the last few years watching the US enrolment cliff inch closer with a mix of fascination and dread. Reports stacked up. Conferences debated it. Boards asked about it. And then, somewhere between the next admissions cycle and the next budget meeting, it slipped down the priority list again.

That window has now closed. Beginning with the 2025/26 academic year, the number of US high school graduates enters a sustained decline that runs through 2041. The Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education estimates a 13% drop nationally, with sharper falls in the Northeast and Midwest where small private colleges and tuition-reliant regional publics are most densely clustered.

Here is the part that should worry institutional leaders most. This is not a cyclical dip. It is demographic. The students who would have walked into US classrooms in 2030 were already born, or not born, 15 years ago. There is no recovery scenario. No marketing campaign and no policy reset will conjure them into existence.

For colleagues outside the US who have lived through their own demographic squeezes, none of this will sound new. What may be less obvious is how quickly the conversation inside American institutions is shifting from “should we recruit more international students” to “we cannot balance the books without them.”

For most of the last two decades, international enrollment in the US was treated as an enrichment strategy. It diversified classrooms, it sharpened global research links, and yes, it contributed meaningfully to net tuition. But it was rarely positioned as core enrollment infrastructure. Domestic undergraduates were the base. International students were the upside.

The cliff inverts that logic. As the domestic 18 to 22 year old population contracts, international recruitment becomes one of the very few levers that actually expands the addressable demand pool, rather than just reshuffling shares within a shrinking one.

Adult learners, online students, and transfer pathways all matter, but they are largely competing for the same domestic population. International demand is a different pool altogether, shaped by demographic and aspirational dynamics in South Asia, Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia that look very different from the US picture.

This has practical consequences for anyone reading The PIE News. International offices that have spent years justifying their budgets through soft metrics now find themselves at the center of institutional financial planning. Partnerships, pathway programs, and offshore recruitment infrastructure are increasingly being discussed in finance committee meetings, not just in international affairs.

International offices that have spent years justifying their budgets through soft metrics now find themselves at the center of institutional financial planning

It also raises uncomfortable questions. Are our institutions actually built to serve international students at scale, or are we still bolting them onto a domestic operating model? Are admissions processes, faculty workloads, housing, mental health support, and post-study career services ready for a student mix that may look fundamentally different by 2030? Across the institutions we work with on both sides of this conversation, the honest answer is not yet.

The window for getting this right is narrow. The next three to four years will determine which institutions enter the deep contraction of the 2030s from a position of agency, and which enter it under constraint. The data is fixed. The leadership choices are not.

For everyone who has spent a career arguing that international education is a strategic discipline and not a side function, this is the moment that argument finally lands. The cliff is here. The institutions that endure will not be the largest or the oldest. They will be the ones that treat global student mobility as core, not optional.

title: Capability for higher education
summary: by Gavin Moodie and Leesa Wheelahan The developers of the capabilities approach Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum argued that education is fundamental to expanding peoples’ capacity to understand and act in the world and thus lead the kind of lives … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Gavin Moodie and Leesa Wheelahan

The developers of the capabilities approach Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum argued that education is fundamental to expanding peoples’ capacity to understand and act in the world and thus lead the kind of lives they value and have reason to value.

Capability for education is the freedom to choose a curriculum or a course one has reason to value, that will support students to develop their emerging conceptions of how they want to live their lives, and provide them with the educational foundation that is necessary to do so. This offers higher education an alternative rationale to human capital theory that has dominated post-secondary education since the Robbins Report of 1963, but which has been losing its appeal as the return on investment in higher education has been plateauing.

Moreover, the value of and confidence in qualifications, particularly higher education qualifications, has been diminishing because they are perceived to no longer deliver on the promise of a good job with good career prospects. If the value of higher education qualifications (and indeed, all educational qualifications) are evaluated only by the extent to which they ‘deliver’ on labour market outcomes, then their value will be questioned. However, qualifications have multiple purposes which, of course, include, but cannot be limited to, labour market outcomes.

Students’ capabilities are advanced by higher education with multiple complementary values, and this helps us to consider the enduring value of and importance of qualifications. Qualifications have intrinsic value for students to realise their self to ‘be’ in the world and to live a life they have reason to value. Qualifications have educational value for accessing the knowledge needed for students to participate in debates and controversies in society and in their field of practice and to proceed to higher levels of education.

Qualifications have use value as a necessary foundation for an occupation and an occupational identity, and exchange value to access the labour market and contribute to an occupational identity. Qualifications also have social value for democratic, socially inclusive communities and society. These different forms of value lead us to posit that qualifications for the capability approach have four purposes, while recognising that different types of qualifications will fulfil these purposes in different ways:

Individual, to develop individuals’ agency to live lives they have reason to value, and to contribute to their families, communities, society, and occupation;

Educational, to develop graduates’ and society’s understanding of theoretical, abstract knowledge;

Occupational, to develop graduates’ individual and work groups’ collective productive capacity; and

Social, to advance society, and social justice and inclusion.

Education should include students’ capability for voice – the capacity to express their wishes, expectations, desires, and concerns, and to have them count when decisions concerning themselves are made. Bonvin related the capability for voice to Appadurai’s ‘capacity to aspire’ or ‘to project oneself in the future’. A capacity to aspire is important because people adapt their preferences according to what they perceive to be achievable. In contrast, education should take account of students’ different capacities and aim to develop their capacity to transform themselves, to increase their agency, to expand their choices about how they wish to live. Thus, ‘the development of capabilities requires the ability to construct one’s preferences (capacity to aspire), to voice them and make them count (capability for voice)’.

Post-secondary education should seek to develop students’ voice in their education, work and wider society. Education should extend its application of these principles to the workplaces where students undertake work integrated or work-based learning. However, trainees may have less scope to exercise their voice at work than on campus.

Collective capabilities

Sen argued that ‘[T]he basic building blocks’ of the capabilities approach is ‘the freedoms of individuals’. Sen is interested in expanding individual liberties and he called his book developing his capabilities approach Development as freedom. But individuals’ freedoms and capabilities are constituted not just by their individual circumstances, but by their membership of social institutions which themselves have varying capabilities. Most basically, the social institution of the family greatly affects members’ capabilities, and reproduces not only people, but differentiated capabilities of successive generations of family members.

Yet families have their own capabilities depending, for example, on their literacy and levels of education, which in turn provides different resources upon which family members can draw. Families have unequal levels of economic, social and cultural capital, which is shaped by relations of class, gender and race and other dimensions of power. Education is collective in three ways, through peers, occupations, and social change. The peer effect is a social multiplier, whereby adults share knowledge with their neighbours and those with whom they interact, developing their peers’ knowledge. This educative role is also collective in building social institutions such as schooling, participating in post-secondary education, and credentialing, although some have argued credentialing has been excessively institutionalised. Education’s educative role is also collective in developing educational organisations such as libraries, educative websites, public lectures, and community education, all of which play a particularly important role in education for adult working learners and other members of the community.

Universities are strongly institutionalised – the idea of a university, of an undergraduate, a lecturer, and a degree are widely understood and reinforced by norms and expectations, despite local variations and changes over time. Universities have strong roles in building and extending social institutions of education and related institutions for the advancement of knowledge and promotion of rational inquiry. Postsecondary education organisations and their staff and students also contribute to the educational, social and cultural leadership of their communities by participating formally and informally in local associations, committees and boards. This develops ‘networks of civic engagement’, which develops communities’ capacity for collective action. Through this post-secondary education institutions anchor their communities by developing knowledge and skills within their region; establishing links and exchanges outside the region; contributing to civic, political, cultural, and social activities and networks in their region; developing facilities and amenities used by the community; and, contributing to their region’s economic activity. Gertler and Vinodrai add that universities foster tolerance, openness and social inclusion:

“First, the university plays an important role in shaping the quality of place and fostering openness and tolerance in the community. Crucial to this process is the ability of the university to create a social environment that is open to dialogue and debate, tolerant of different viewpoints, and accessible to many different social, ethnic, and cultural groups (locally, nationally, and internationally). In other words, the university has a role in reducing ‘barriers to entry’ and working towards social inclusion.”

Capability for higher education at three levels

Thus, higher education develops capabilities at three levels: 1) the individual, 2) social and work groups, and 3) society. Most attention has been given to higher education’s contributions to individuals, and to society. More recently higher education has given attention to teamwork but much of this has been about individuals’ capacity to work in teams rather than the development of the capabilities of groups. The capabilities approach is also strongly applicable to adult, further, and special education, which is the subject of the next in our SRHE Blog series, and of our open access book.

Dr Gavin Moodie is Honorary Research Fellow at the University of Oxford’s Department of Education

Leesa Wheelahan is Professor Emerita and William G. Davis Chair in Community College Leadership Emerita at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, University of Toronto, and Honorary Research Fellow at the University of Oxford’s Department of Education.

title: Eco wins: From death strip to nature haven and other green surprises
summary: A Cold War relic becomes a biodiversity haven, a Pokemon Go for trees and seagrass gets a second life. This week's eco wins come from some unexpected places.
full_text:
After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, the border zone that divided West and East Germany was left largely untouched. Today, the nearly 1,400-kilometer (870 miles) stretch, once known as the death strip, is a "green belt." It's home to around 7,500 species of insects and spiders, hundreds of them endangered, as well as otters, wildcats and birds on the brink of extinction.

Because the military zone was sealed off for decades, species that have vanished elsewhere in Germany were able to take hold here. Now 88% of the area is under protection, and cycle paths and information panels allow visitors to explore what was once completely off-limits.

Read the full story here: East-West border death zone now Germany's biodiversity oasis

An urban tree database

Not all heroes wear capes, but some do form a canopy. Urban trees quietly cool neighborhoods, reduce flooding and improve our wellbeing. But in many cities, trees are under pressure from heat, drought, traffic and too much concrete.

Now, a citizen-science project in Germany is helping people map and monitor the trees around them. Think Pokemon Go, but for urban nature and with real-world benefits for the climate.

Seagrass goes from beach nuisance to building material

On Poel, a German island in the Baltic Sea, washed-up seagrass is being turned into sustainable insulation for homes, while helping clean local beaches in the process.

As demand for eco-friendly construction materials grows, the project is attracting interest from across Europe and could give new value to a resource that was previously viewed as waste.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

title: heise-Angebot: c’t-Webinar: Die faszinierende Welt der Quantenphysik verstehen
summary: Entdecken Sie die faszinierende Welt der Quantenphysik! Das Webinar führt kompakt durch die Grundlagen, von Schrödingers Katze bis zum Quantencomputer.
full_text:
Quantenphysik zieht Menschen weltweit in ihren Bann. Sie folgt einem Modell, das unserer Intuition widerspricht und dessen Interpretation selbst Genies wie Einstein vor große Rätsel stellte: Katzen können gleichzeitig tot und lebendig sein, Teilchen können sich an mehreren Orten zugleich befinden. Doch genau das macht die Quantenphysik so faszinierend. Tief im Inneren schlummert ein Kosmos mit Regeln, die sich grundlegend von denen unseres Alltags unterscheiden. Und obwohl sie nur für die kleinsten Objekte eine Rolle spielt, ist sie überall: im Computer, im Smartphone, im Laser und beim Arzt.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Im Webinar „Grundlagen der Quantenphysik – Von Schrödingers Katze bis zum Quantencomputer“ führt Dr. Sabrina Patsch, c’t-Redakteurin und promovierte Quantenphysikerin, durch die zentralen Konzepte des Fachs. Sie hat an der Freien Universität Berlin promoviert, im Labor des Nobelpreisträgers Serge Haroche am Collège de France geforscht und tritt regelmäßig als Science Slammerin auf.

Von Grundbegriffen bis zu Quantenalgorithmen

Zu Beginn lernen Sie die zentralen Grundbegriffe kennen: Welle-Teilchen-Dualismus, Superposition, Verschränkung und mehr. Im weiteren Verlauf geht es um die erste Quantenrevolution, der wir Laser und Atomuhren verdanken, sowie um die zweite Quantenrevolution mit Quantencomputern, Quantensimulation, Quantenmetrologie und Quantenkommunikation. Daran schließt sich ein Blick auf den Quantencomputer selbst an.

Haben Sie keine Scheu – vielleicht sind Ihnen einige Begriffe schon begegnet, aber bisher unklar geblieben. Das Webinar richtet sich an Menschen, die einen ersten Zugang zur Quantenphysik suchen. Vorkenntnisse in Mathematik oder Programmierung sind nicht erforderlich. Ein grundsätzliches Interesse und physikalisches Schulwissen – etwa zu Atomen, Elektronen und Ionen – erleichtern den Einstieg.

Fragen stellen und Aufzeichnung nutzen

Während der Veranstaltung haben Sie die Möglichkeit, über einen Online-Chat Fragen zu stellen. Sie benötigen lediglich einen aktuellen Browser, um am Webinar teilzunehmen. Falls Sie einmal nicht ganz mitkommen, können Sie die Inhalte später bequem mithilfe der Aufzeichnung und ergänzender Materialien nachvollziehen. Weitere Informationen zur Veranstaltung und zur Anmeldung finden Sie auf der Webinar-Website.

Kosten: 69,00 Euro

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige
translated_text:
Quantum physics captivates people all over the world. It follows a model that contradicts our intuition and whose interpretation posed great puzzles even to geniuses like Einstein: cats can be dead and alive at the same time, particles can be in several places at the same time. But that's exactly what makes quantum physics so fascinating. Deep inside lies a cosmos with rules that are fundamentally different from those of our everyday lives. And although it only plays a role in the smallest objects, it is everywhere: in computers, smartphones, lasers and at the doctor's office.

Read more after the ad

In the webinar “Fundamentals of Quantum Physics – From Schrödinger’s Cat to Quantum Computers” Dr. Sabrina Patsch, c’t editor and PhD in quantum physics, through the central concepts of the subject. She earned her doctorate at the Free University of Berlin, conducted research in the laboratory of Nobel Prize winner Serge Haroche at the Collège de France and regularly appears as a science slammer.

From basic concepts to quantum algorithms

At the beginning you will get to know the central basic concepts: wave-particle dualism, superposition, entanglement and more. The following will be about the first quantum revolution, to which we owe lasers and atomic clocks, as well as the second quantum revolution with quantum computers, quantum simulation, quantum metrology and quantum communication. This is followed by a look at the quantum computer itself.

Don't be afraid - you may have already come across some terms but have remained unclear until now. The webinar is aimed at people who are looking for initial access to quantum physics. No prior knowledge of mathematics or programming is required. A basic interest and school knowledge of physics - for example about atoms, electrons and ions - make it easier to get started.

Ask questions and use recording
